newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nigeria says U.N. team will not meet detainees.
newsitem.headline: Nigeria says U.N. team will not meet detainees.

text.p: Two United Nations human rights investigators due to visit Nigeria next week will not meet political detainees, a senior official said in remarks reported by local newspapers on Wednesday.

"Their mandate is restrictive and specific," Anwalu Yadudu, special adviser to the Nigerian military ruler on legal matters was quoted as saying. "Their mandate restricts them to independence of judges, extra-judicial killings and summary execution of accused persons."

Bacre Waly Ndiaye, U.N. special rapporteur on extrajudicial, summary or arbitrary executions and Param Cumaraswamy, U.N. special rapporteur on the independence of judges and lawyers, are due in Nigeria from February 23 to March 5.

They have been seeking access to Nigeria since the hanging in 1995 of nine Ogoni minority rights activists including author Ken Saro-Wiwa. Nigeria drew worldwide outrage over the hangings of the activists after their conviction in the 1994 murder of four pro-government tribal chiefs.
Their trial was judged unfair by international judicial experts and 19 Ogoni youths facing similar charges are still in detention.
Also in detention is millionaire Moshood Abiola, who is charged with treason and has been held since 1994 when he proclaimed himself president in defiance of the army rulers.
He is widely believed to have won a 1993 presidential poll annulled by a previous army government.
A U.N. statement in Geneva last week announcing the visit said the U.N. investigators expected full access to detainees and non-governmental organisations.

But Yadudu said the rapporteurs' mandate did not extend to meeting detainees. "As far as the government is concerned we will deal with them according to their mandate which is categorical and specific according to the U.N. resolution."

The investigators will report back to the U.N. Human Rights Commission. Nigeria will be one of the countries in the dock when the main U.N. human rights forum opens its annual six-week meeting in Geneva on March 10, according to U.N. sources.
The 53-member body last April censured Nigeria for violating fundamental freedoms of its citizens and called on Abuja to allow the two U.N. investigators to make a joint visit.
